transcript.answer:
Summary (root cause)
- The rollout of ledger-api v1.4.2 triggered a file-descriptor exhaustion in some pods. A subset of pods (all those scheduled onto node rcabench-worker2) hit "[Errno 24] Too many open files", stopped accepting connections and failed readiness probes — those pods became NotReady. Pods on rcabench-worker remained healthy.
- Short version: the app in 1.4.2 is exhausting file descriptors on rcabench-worker2 (EMFILE), causing readiness probe failures and NotReady pods.

What I checked
- Pod status (namespace=ledger):
  - Deployment: ledger-api (replicas: 6, available: 3)
  - ReplicaSet: ledger-api-866db84748 (replicas: 6, available: 3)
  - Pods (ledger-api-866db84748-...):
    - ledger-api-866db84748-2zjp4 — READY=false — node=rcabench-worker2 — IMAGE=python:3.12-alpine
    - ledger-api-866db84748-cz4wp — READY=false — node=rcabench-worker2
    - ledger-api-866db84748-vv6jk — READY=false — node=rcabench-worker2
    - ledger-api-866db84748-md6xh — READY=true — node=rcabench-worker
    - ledger-api-866db84748-r5mbh — READY=true — node=rcabench-worker
    - ledger-api-866db84748-xzjxb — READY=true — node=rcabench-worker

- Events (last ~1 hour) around rollout (09:43:20Z):
  - New replica set/Pods created for v1.4.2; readiness probe failures: "Readiness probe failed: Get "http://<podIP>:8080/healthz": dial tcp <podIP>:8080: connect: connection refused"
  - Later for the same pods: "Readiness probe failed: HTTP probe failed with statuscode: 503"

- Application logs (last 30 minutes) from a NotReady pod (ledger-api-866db84748-2zjp4):
  - startup: "2026-10-07T09:44:13Z INFO ledger-api starting version=1.4.2"
  - repeated errors every ~10s: "ERROR ledger-api accept failed: [Errno 24] Too many open files" (dozens of occurrences between ~09:45:33Z and 09:57:13Z)

- Logs from a Ready pod (ledger-api-866db84748-md6xh) only show startup: "INFO ledger-api starting version=1.4.2" — no EMFILE errors.

Why this is the root cause
1. The app process logs show EMFILE on the NotReady pods — this is a direct OS error meaning the process attempted to open more file descriptors than allowed.
2. When accept() fails due to EMFILE the process can't accept new connections → readiness probe (HTTP /healthz) cannot be served → kubelet marks pod Unhealthy/NotReady.
3. The problem is node-local: failing pods are all on rcabench-worker2 while pods on rcabench-worker are healthy. That implies either:
   - the node (rcabench-worker2) has lower per-process or system-wide FD limits, or
   - something on that node is consuming many FDs (other processes/containers) and the new pods hit the aggregate limit, or
   - the app in 1.4.2 opened significantly more FDs and only pods colocated with other consumers or with stricter limits failed.

Confidence: high that the immediate cause is FD exhaustion (EMFILE). The precise reason why only rcabench-worker2 is affected (node config vs. colocation) requires node-level checks.

Evidence (exact lines)
- Pod logs (ledger-api-866db84748-2zjp4, last 30m):
  - "2026-10-07T09:44:13Z INFO ledger-api starting version=1.4.2"
  - "2026-10-07T09:45:33Z ERROR ledger-api accept failed: [Errno 24] Too many open files"
  - (repeated every ~10s up to 2026-10-07T09:57:13Z)
- Events:
  - "2026-10-07T09:43:21Z Warning Unhealthy ledger-api-66778d957c-57vrw Readiness probe failed: Get "http://10.244.1.10:8080/healthz": dial tcp 10.244.1.10:8080: connect: connection refused"
  - similar readiness failures for the 866db84748 pods and later "HTTP probe failed with statuscode: 503"

Immediate recommended actions (safe, quick)
1. Roll back the deployment to the previous working image (if you want to restore service quickly):
   - kubectl rollout undo deployment/ledger-api -n ledger
   - Or explicitly set image to the prior tag in the deployment and kubectl apply.
   (This removes the new behavior that is causing escalated FD usage.)

2. Short-term mitigation if rollback not possible:
   - Cordon rcabench-worker2 to avoid placing further pods there:
     - kubectl cordon rcabench-worker2
   - Optionally drain (careful, this causes rescheduling): kubectl drain rcabench-worker2 --ignore-daemonsets --delete-emptydir-data
   - This will move pods to other nodes where they are not failing (but only if capacity exists).

3. If you accept node admin work: increase allowed file-descriptors on the node (host-level).
   - On the node(s), increase per-process soft/hard nofile (systemd unit for container runtime or process system limits). Example (on node, requires sudo):
     - check current per-process limit: cat /proc/<pid>/limits | grep "Max open files"
     - check system limit: cat /proc/sys/fs/file-max
     - raise limits via /etc/security/limits.conf or systemd drop-in for container runtime (e.g. for containerd/docker) and restart the runtime.
   - Note: containers inherit limits from the host runtime; Kubernetes does not directly expose ulimit in Pod spec.

Further diagnosis commands (run these now)
- To re-check distribution and which pods are failing:
  - kubectl get pods -n ledger -o wide

- To see the exact pod logs I inspected (30 minutes window):
  - kubectl logs -n ledger ledger-api-866db84748-2zjp4 --since=30m
  - kubectl logs -n ledger ledger-api-866db84748-md6xh --since=30m

- To check FD usage from inside a container (compare failing vs. healthy):
  - kubectl exec -n ledger -it ledger-api-866db84748-2zjp4 -- sh -c 'ulimit -n && ls -1 /proc/1/fd | wc -l'
  - kubectl exec -n ledger -it ledger-api-866db84748-md6xh -- sh -c 'ulimit -n && ls -1 /proc/1/fd | wc -l'
  (This shows the process's ulimit and how many fds it currently has open.)

- Node-level checks (requires node access):
  - kubectl describe node rcabench-worker2
  - On the node (ssh), for the ledger-api container process pid:
    - sudo ls -l /proc/<pid>/fd | wc -l
    - sudo cat /proc/<pid>/limits | grep "Max open files"
    - cat /proc/sys/fs/file-max

Long-term fixes to consider
- Fix the root cause in the app if 1.4.2 introduced a leak or higher concurrency: ensure sockets/files are closed, reduce per-connection FDs, or pool reuse.
- Add an application-side limit or backpressure to avoid unbounded FD growth.
- If the app legitimately needs more FDs, raise the host/runtime limits (systemd + container runtime) and document required capacity.
- Add pod anti-affinity (spread across nodes) so you don't place many replicas on a single node.
- Add more thorough startup and readiness handling: if the app is temporarily out of fds, it should fail fast or degrade gracefully rather than continuously accepting and leaking.
- Add health-check / metrics to expose FD usage so you catch this earlier.

Final notes / next steps I can run for you
- I can:
  - fetch fd counts from inside a selected pod (need confirmation which pod to run into),
  - describe the node(s) and show any node conditions or kubelet events,
  - re-run logs for any other pod/time window.
- If you want an immediate rollback I can show the exact kubectl commands or perform those steps (confirm and I will proceed).

If you want me to keep investigating (e.g., confirm host ulimits on rcabench-worker2 or inspect other processes on that node), tell me whether I should attempt node-level checks (requires node access/privileges) or prefer cluster-level actions (rollback/cordon).
